article.headline: Amgen Nears Record As Earnings Rebound And Trial Data Draw Notice
article.deck: The seven-week cup's buy point is 447.13 with a buy range to 469.49; the stock closed 3.3% below it, still setting up.
body: Amgen makes drugs for chronic and serious disease and sells them worldwide. Its lineup includes Enbrel for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, Otezla for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, Prolia for postmenopausal osteoporosis, XGEVA to prevent bone complications, Repatha to cut the risk of heart attack and stroke, and Nplate. It is a large, established drugmaker, not a story stock, and the chart has been acting like a leader anyway.

The earnings explain why. June-quarter EPS rose 64.9% to 4.37 on revenue up 9.5% to $10.05 billion. That followed EPS of 3.34 in the March quarter and 2.45 in the December quarter, so profit has risen two quarters in a row. Revenue climbed from $8.62 billion in March to $10.05 billion in June. The September 2025 quarter showed EPS of 5.93, a high bar for the next report, due Nov. 3.
The market values Amgen at $233.8 billion. The stock trades at 26.9 times trailing earnings and 17.7 times forward earnings, a lower multiple than either payments name on today's breakout list.

Shares are up 32.1% this year, 45.5% over 12 months and 13.9% in the past month. Amgen holds RS rank 90 of 99 on the desk's list, and its RS line sits 2.6% below its high. It is one of the leaders in healthcare, the fourth-strongest group on the desk's board, alongside Exelixis.

The chart shows a seven-week cup that ran 16.2% deep, from an Aug. 25 rim to a Sept. 16 low at 374.46. The buy point is 447.13, ten cents over the 52-week high of 447.03, and the buy range runs to 469.49. Friday the stock fell 1.54, or 0.4%, to 432.49, 3.3% under the buy point. Volume ran 0.93 times the 50-day average.

The trend underneath is sound. The stock is 4.2% above its 50-day line at 415.01, 17.2% above its 200-day line at 368.90, and 1.58 ATRs above the 21-day line at 414.56. The right side of the cup has been built in a market the desk rates in correction.
A Wednesday headline asked what a 70% remission trial result could mean for Amgen's pipeline. The stock has no breakout yet, and the Nov. 3 report is the next scheduled test.
article.watch: Watch for a decisive close above 447.13 and the Nov. 3 earnings report.

corner.topic: The 7-8% sell rule: why every position starts with a stop and how to set it from the buy point
corner.headline: The 7%-8% Sell Rule: Set The Stop Before You Buy
corner.deck: Hewlett Packard Enterprise's Oct. 1 breakout shows why every position needs a loss limit tied to the buy point from the first day.
body: The sell rule is the simplest in the method and the one most often broken. When a stock bought at or near its buy point falls 7% to 8% below the price paid, it is sold. No waiting for a bounce, no averaging down, no new reason to stay. The rule exists because the losses that wreck accounts start out as small ones.

The stop is set before the order goes in, and it is set from the buy point. If you buy a stock at its buy point, the 7%-8% line sits 7% to 8% under that price. If you buy higher in the buy range, your cushion to the stop line shrinks, because the stop is measured from what you paid. That is one reason the buy range is capped at 5% above the buy point: chase further and the normal shakeout in a new move can take you out.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise shows the rule at work. The stock built a 17-week deep cup that ran 36.6% from a June 2 rim to a July 2 low. The buy point was 64.35, and the stock broke out past it on Oct. 1. The breakout session traded 0.79 times its 50-day volume average. The stock carried RS rank 96 of 99 on the desk's list, and its July quarter showed EPS up 404.8% on revenue up 33.7%. By the numbers, it was a leader.

Eleven sessions later, it closed Friday at 55.13, 14.3% under the 64.35 buy point, after a 6.0% drop on the day. It is 7.1% under its 50-day line at 59.37. Headlines said the stock plunged 20% this week as AI financing worries extended a hardware selloff.

A buyer at 64.35 who honored the rule took a loss of 7% to 8% somewhere on the way down and was out. A buyer who did not is now down 14.3% from the buy point, nearly double the limit, and needs a larger percentage gain than that just to get back to even. That asymmetry is the whole case for the rule: every point of loss takes more than a point of gain to recover, and the gap widens the deeper the hole.

The rule did not require knowing anything about AI financing. It did not require reading the news at all. The price said the breakout had failed, and the stop turned that into a small, defined loss. Palo Alto Networks and Micron, both in today's stories, show the same pattern: Palo Alto closed 14.3% under its 398.98 buy point and Micron 15.2% under its 1036.23 buy point.
The 7%-8% figure is a maximum, not a target. In a market the desk rates in correction, as it does now, many traders cut losses sooner. The rule never moves the other way.
takeaways: Set the stop before you buy, 7% to 8% below your purchase price.
Buying high in the buy range shrinks the room between your price and the stop.
HPE broke out past 64.35 on Oct. 1 and closed 14.3% below it 11 sessions later.
Strong earnings and a high RS rank do not protect a failed breakout.
Small losses are recoverable; letting them double is how accounts get hurt.
